items.prompt: Which HTML element is intended to hold the main navigation links of a page?

options.label: <header>
<section>
<aside>
<nav>

rubric: <nav> is the semantic element for major navigation blocks.
<header> is a common confusion, but it is for introductory content and may or may not contain navigation.

items.prompt: Which CSS property sets the space between an element's border and its content?

options.label: outline
margin
padding
gap

rubric: Padding is the space inside the border around the content.
Margin is outside the border, a frequent mix-up.

items.prompt: Which CSS declaration turns an element into a flex container?

options.label: flex: container;
display: flex;
float: flex;
position: flex;

rubric: display: flex creates a flex container.
The other values are not valid ways to enable flexbox.

items.prompt: Which HTML tag is used for the largest, top-level heading on a page?

options.label: <title>
<head>

rubric: <h1> is the top-level heading.
<title> sets the browser tab title, and <head> holds metadata.

items.prompt: What does the CSS selector `.card` match?

options.label: Elements with class="card"
Elements named <card>
Elements whose text is "card"
Elements with id="card"

rubric: A dot prefix selects by class.
A hash prefix would select by id; a bare name selects tags.

items.prompt: Which of the following are semantic HTML5 elements? Select all that apply.

options.label: <footer>
<div>
<span>
<main>

items.prompt:
You are writing a stylesheet and want a rule to apply to every

element on the page. You recall that CSS rules consist of a selector and a block of declarations. Which rule is written correctly?

options.label: p ( color = blue )
p { color: blue; }
p: color { blue; }
{ color: blue }

rubric: A selector followed by braces with property: value; pairs is valid CSS.
The others mix up syntax from other languages or HTML.

items.prompt: Why is a <button> preferred over a <div> with a click handler for a clickable control?

options.label: It is focusable and keyboard-operable by default, and assistive tech announces it
It needs no CSS or JavaScript to work, whereas a div always needs both to be clickable
It loads faster because browsers skip style calculation and layout work for button elements
It always stops the page from reloading, since buttons never submit or navigate anywhere

rubric: Native buttons provide built-in accessibility and keyboard behavior.
Speed or reload claims are misconceptions.

items.prompt: An element has width: 200px, padding: 20px and a 5px border, with the default content-box sizing. How wide is the space it occupies, excluding margin?

options.label: 200px
245px
225px
250px

rubric: Content-box adds padding and border on both sides: 200+40+10=250.
200px ignores them; 225 counts one side; 245 omits a border side.

items.prompt: Two rules set the color of the same paragraph: `p { color: red; }` and `.note { color: green; }`. The paragraph has class="note". What color is the text, and why?

options.label: Red, because the first matching rule always wins
Red, because tag selectors are more basic and apply first
Green, because a class selector is more specific than a tag selector
Green, because it was written later in the file

rubric: Specificity: class beats element regardless of order.
Distractors assume order or first-match decides.

items.prompt: In a flex container with `flex-direction: row`, what does `justify-content: center` do?

options.label: Makes every item the same width as its siblings
Centers the items along the horizontal main axis
Centers the text inside each item
Centers the items along the vertical cross axis of the container

rubric: justify-content aligns along the main axis, horizontal for row.
align-items handles the cross axis, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` for responsive pages?

options.label: It hides content that does not fit on a small screen
It sets the CSS breakpoints used by media queries
It makes the layout width match the device screen instead of a zoomed-out desktop width
It forces the page to resize itself when the user rotates the phone

rubric: It tells mobile browsers to use the device width for layout.
It doesn't define breakpoints or hide content.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the CSS grid layout? Select all that apply.

options.label: Items must be placed using floats
The `fr` unit shares leftover space in proportion
It can only lay out items in a single line
It arranges items in rows and columns at the same time

rubric: Grid is two-dimensional and fr divides free space.
Single-line layout describes flexbox; floats are not needed for grid.

items.prompt: A learner builds a page with three <div> boxes in a row using `display: flex`. On a narrow phone screen the boxes are squeezed into thin columns. They want the boxes to stack vertically on small screens. Which approach fits?

options.label: Remove the viewport meta tag so the phone zooms the page out
Add `float: left` to every box so they wrap onto new lines
Use a max-width media query to set `flex-direction: column`
Set a fixed 1000px width on the container so boxes keep size

rubric: Media queries adapt layout by screen width; column direction stacks items.
Fixed widths and removing viewport worsen small-screen layout.

items.prompt: Which element best marks up a block of links that lets visitors move between the main pages of a site?

options.label: `<section>`
`<aside>`
`<nav>`
`<div>`

rubric: `<nav>` is the semantic element for major navigation links.
`<div>` and `<section>` are generic or thematic grouping elements and carry no navigation meaning.

items.prompt: What does `box-sizing: border-box` change about an element that has a set `width`?

options.label: The width includes the margin as well as padding and border
The width applies only to the content area of the box
The width excludes padding but includes the border
The width includes the padding and border

rubric: With border-box, the declared width covers content, padding and border.
Margin is never part of the width, and 'content area only' describes the default content-box.

items.prompt: Which of these elements is displayed as a block-level element by default?

options.label: `<span>`
`<strong>`

rubric:
`

` starts on a new line and fills the available width.
`<span>`, `<a>` and `<strong>` are inline by default.

items.prompt: A container has `display: flex` and no other flex properties. How are its three child boxes laid out?

options.label: They overlap at the top-left corner of the container
They sit side by side in a row along the main axis, starting at the start edge
They stack vertically, each on its own line, like normal block elements
They are placed into a grid with equal rows and columns

rubric: The default flex-direction is row, so children line up horizontally.
Stacking is the non-flex block behaviour; flex does not create a grid or overlap items.

items.prompt: Why should an informative `` have an `alt` attribute?

options.label: It scales the image to fit its container when the screen is narrow
It shows a tooltip with the image description when the mouse hovers over it
It tells search engines not to index the image file or show it in results
It gives screen readers text for the image and shows if it fails to load

rubric: `alt` is the text alternative used by assistive tech and shown when the image is missing.
Tooltips come from `title`, and scaling is done with CSS.

items.prompt: Which of the following elements are semantic, meaning their names describe the role of their content? Select all that apply.

options.label: `<footer>`
`<span>`
`<article>`
`<div>`
`<figure>`

rubric: `<article>`, `<footer>` and `<figure>` each describe what their content is.
`<div>` and `<span>` are generic containers with no meaning.

items.prompt:
A stylesheet contains `.note { color: green; }` first, then later `p { color: blue; }`. The page has `

Hello

`. What colour is the text, and why?

options.label: Black, because conflicting rules cancel out and the default applies
Green, because a class selector is more specific than an element selector
Blue, because element selectors target the tag directly and are most specific
Blue, because the rule written later in the file always wins

rubric: Specificity is checked before source order, and a class outranks an element selector.
Choosing blue assumes the later rule always wins, ignoring specificity.

items.prompt: With default `box-sizing`, a div has `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid;`. How wide is its rendered box, excluding margin?

options.label: 200px
250px
240px
225px

rubric: 240px forgets the border and 225px counts only one side of padding and border.

items.prompt: You want a rule to apply only when the viewport is 600px wide or narrower. Which media query does this?

options.label: `@media (max-height: 600px)`
`@media (min-width: 600px)`
`@media (max-width: 600px)`
`@media (width: 600px)`

rubric: `max-width: 600px` matches viewports up to and including 600px.
`min-width` reverses the direction, `width` matches exactly 600px, and height tests the wrong dimension.

items.prompt: Which declarations on a flex container centre a single child both horizontally and vertically (default row direction)?

options.label: `margin: center; align-self: center;`
`justify-content: center; align-items: center;`
`text-align: center; vertical-align: middle;`
`align-content: center; justify-items: center;`

rubric: In a row, justify-content centres on the main axis and align-items on the cross axis.
The other options use properties that don't centre a lone flex item or are invalid.

items.prompt: Which declaration creates a grid with three equal-width columns?

options.label: `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);`
`grid-template-columns: 3fr;`
`grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr);`
`grid-columns: 3 equal;`

rubric: `repeat(3, 1fr)` makes three columns sharing space equally.
`3fr` is one column, `grid-columns` is not a property, and rows are not columns.

items.prompt: Two block siblings sit in normal flow. The first has `margin-bottom: 30px`, the second `margin-top: 20px`. What is the vertical gap between them?

options.label: 10px
20px
50px
30px

rubric: Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger value, 30px.
50px assumes margins add, which does not happen when they collapse.

items.prompt: Given `Go`, which selectors match this element? Select all that apply.

options.label: #btn
.primary .btn
.btn.primary
.btn
a.primary

rubric: `.btn`, `a.primary` and `.btn.primary` all describe this element's tag and classes.
`#btn` needs an id, and `.primary .btn` needs `.btn` inside a `.primary` ancestor.

items.prompt: A page has a flex container holding three cards, each with `flex: 1`. On a phone the cards are squeezed too narrow to read. You want them to drop onto new lines when each would be under about 200px wide. Which change does this?

options.label: Set `overflow: hidden` on the container so extra width is cut off
Set `align-content: wrap` on the container and `min-width: 200px` on the cards
Set `flex-wrap: wrap` on the container and `flex: 1 1 200px` on the cards
Set `flex-direction: column` on the container and `width: 200px` on the cards

rubric: Wrapping plus a 200px flex-basis lets cards move to new rows when space runs out.
The other options hide content, use an invalid value, or use the wrong property for wrapping.

items.prompt: A block has `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid;` and `box-sizing: border-box`. What is the width of its content area?

options.label: 150px
160px
200px
240px

rubric: With border-box, the 200px includes padding and border: 200 - 40 - 10 = 150px.
240px and 210px-style answers come from assuming content-box; 160px forgets the border.

items.prompt: A flex container is 600px wide with no gap. It holds three items with `flex: 1`, `flex: 1` and `flex: 2` (basis 0). What are their widths in order?

options.label: 120px, 120px and 360px
100px, 100px and 400px
150px, 150px and 300px
200px, 200px and 200px

rubric: The free space is split in a 1:1:2 ratio, giving 150, 150 and 300.
Equal widths ignore the grow factors; the other options use wrong ratios.

items.prompt: A grid container is 640px wide and uses `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 20px;`. How wide is each column?

options.label: 187px
180px
213px
200px

rubric: Two gaps take 40px, leaving 600px for three columns: 200px each.
213px ignores the gaps; 187px subtracts a gap per column.

items.prompt:
A `

` sits inside a `div`. The CSS has `div p.note { color: blue; }`, then `#intro { color: red; }`, then `.note { color: green; }` last. What colour is the text?

options.label: black
red
green
blue

rubric: The id selector (1,0,0) outranks the class and element selectors regardless of order.
Blue assumes more selector parts win; green assumes the last rule wins.

items.prompt: Which markup correctly pairs an image with a visible caption in semantic HTML?

options.label:
`
`
`Hoover Dam`
``
``

rubric: `figcaption` is valid only inside `figure`, which gives the caption its association.
`caption` belongs to tables and `legend` to fieldsets; figcaption in a div is invalid.

items.prompt: A `.card` has `width: 300px` and is a block element inside a wider parent. Which approaches centre it horizontally in the parent? Select all that apply.

options.label: Parent `display: flex; justify-content: center;`
`.card { text-align: center; }`
Parent `display: grid; justify-content: center;`
`.card { margin: 0 auto; }`
Parent `display: flex; align-items: center;`

rubric: Auto side margins, flex main-axis centring and grid justify-content all centre the box horizontally.
`text-align` only centres inline content inside the card; `align-items` centres on the cross axis (vertical in a row).

items.prompt: A page has a header, a short `main` and a footer in `body`. On tall monitors the footer floats mid-screen with blank space below. You want it at the viewport bottom on short pages but pushed down by content on long pages. Which CSS achieves this?

options.label: `body { height: 100vh; }` and `footer { margin-top: auto; }`, which pushes the footer down in normal block flow
`footer { position: fixed; bottom: 0; }`, which keeps it pinned to the viewport bottom at all times, even over content
`body { display: flex; flex-direction: column; min-height: 100vh; }` and `main { flex: 1; }`
`main { height: 100%; }` with no changes to `body` or `html`, so main fills the remaining space

rubric: A column flex body with min-height and a growing main pushes the footer down yet lets it move with long content.
Fixed positioning overlaps content; auto margins and percentage heights fail without a flex context or defined parent height.

items.prompt: A `.panel` has no padding or border and contains an `h2` with `margin-top: 40px`. The 40px gap appears above the panel's background, and the heading touches the panel's top edge. What explains this?

options.label: Block elements inside a container usually apply vertical margins only at the bottom edge, so the top margin moves to the parent
The panel has `overflow: visible`, so the child's margin is drawn as extra parent padding above the content and shifts the heading
The h2's top margin collapses through the parent's top edge, as nothing separates them, so it sits outside the panel
The h2's margin is dropped when its parent is a block element without a set height, so the panel keeps just its own margin

rubric: Parent and first-child vertical margins collapse when no padding, border or new formatting context separates them.
Distractors invent rules about ignored margins or overflow; margins are not ignored, they collapse.

items.prompt: A badge with `position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0;` should sit in the corner of its `.card`, but it lands in the top-right corner of the page. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: No ancestor is positioned, so the badge uses the page's initial containing block; `.card` needs `position: relative`
`top` and `right` only take effect with `position: fixed`, so the badge has to be switched to fixed positioning there
`.card` must be `display: block` before absolutely positioned children can use it as their reference box for offsets
Without a `z-index` the badge is resolved against the page instead of its card, so adding `z-index: 1` anchors it

rubric: Absolute elements are offset from the nearest positioned ancestor, falling back to the initial containing block.
z-index and display do not set the containing block; fixed positioning would tie it to the viewport.

items.prompt: A dropdown with `z-index: 9999` inside `.sidebar` (`position: relative; z-index: 1`) still paints below `.content` (`position: relative; z-index: 2`). Why?

options.label: The dropdown's z-index only competes inside the sidebar's stacking context, and that whole context ranks below `.content`
z-index values above 999 are capped by browsers, so 9999 falls back to auto and the dropdown loses to `.content`
z-index only orders elements within one parent, so siblings of `.sidebar` always paint above everything inside it
`position: relative` on the sidebar resets its children's z-index to zero, so the dropdown ranks beneath `.content`

rubric: A positioned element with z-index creates a stacking context; children cannot escape its rank among siblings.
The distractors invent caps, resets or sibling rules that browsers do not apply.

items.prompt: Nested lists use `ul { font-size: 0.9em; }`. The top list looks fine, but each deeper level is visibly smaller. What is the cause?

options.label: `em` resolves against the root font size, so deeper lists are scaled by their distance from the `html` element
`em` resolves against the parent's computed font size, so each nested `ul` shrinks the text again by another 10%
Each nested `ul` is more specific than the one above, so the cascade multiplies the font-size values together
Browsers apply `ul` font-size rules once per page, so deeper lists fall back to a smaller default text size

rubric: Font-size in em is relative to the parent's computed size, so repeated application compounds; `rem` avoids this.
Specificity does not multiply values, and `em` is not tied to the root (that is `rem`).

items.prompt: `.hero { height: 50%; }` sits inside `.wrap`, which has no height set, inside `body`. The hero collapses to its content height. Why?

options.label: A percentage height resolves only against a parent with a definite height; with an auto-height parent it behaves as `auto`
Percentage heights are measured against the viewport width, so a hero in an auto-height container ends up with zero height
`height` percentages are ignored on block elements unless the element itself also has `display: flex` applied to it
`.wrap` needs `overflow: hidden`, otherwise child percentage heights are measured against the content and drop out

rubric: Percent heights need a parent whose height does not depend on its content.
The distractors misattribute the behaviour to viewport width, display or overflow.

items.prompt: A page scrolls sideways on a 375px-wide phone. Which of these could be causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: An image set to `width: 800px` with no `max-width`
A `.banner { width: 100%; padding: 0 16px; }` using the default `box-sizing: content-box`
A global `* { box-sizing: border-box; }` rule
Images styled with `max-width: 100%; height: auto`

rubric: Content-box plus padding makes the banner wider than its container, and a fixed 800px image overflows the viewport.
Border-box and max-width: 100% are common fixes, not causes.

items.prompt: A grid uses `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)`. One card holds a 60-character URL with no spaces, and that column becomes much wider than the others, which squeeze. What best explains this behaviour?

options.label: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, so a column cannot shrink below its content's min-content width; `minmax(0, 1fr)` lets it shrink
Grid items default to `overflow: hidden`, which forces the column to grow until the whole unbroken text can be revealed
`repeat(3, 1fr)` creates columns whose size is fixed by the widest item in any row, so one long URL resizes all three tracks
`fr` units share space in proportion to content length, so the column holding the longest item gets a larger fraction of the space

rubric: The automatic minimum of a 1fr track is the item's min-content size, so unbreakable text props the column open.
The other options invent content-proportional fr sizing or overflow defaults.

items.prompt: A flex row has `display: flex` and three children with `flex: 1`. One child contains a 60-character unbroken URL, and that column overflows the container while the others shrink. Which explains this?

options.label: Flex containers ignore `overflow` on children, so the long string forces the row to grow
A flex item's automatic minimum width equals its min-content width, so it cannot shrink below the unbroken string
The `flex-basis` of 0% is computed from text length, so the child with more characters gets a larger share
`flex: 1` sets `flex-shrink: 0` on every child, so the item holding the longer text refuses to shrink at all and overflows

rubric: Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which prevents shrinking below min-content; `min-width: 0` fixes it.
Distractors misread what `flex: 1` sets or invent text-based basis calculations.

items.prompt: A `div` with a background colour contains an `h2` with `margin-top: 40px`. The div has no padding or border. The 40px gap appears above the div's background instead of inside it. What explains this?

options.label: The h2's top margin collapses with the div's top margin, so the combined space sits outside the div's background
The h2 is out of normal flow because headings are floated by default, so its margin applies relative to the viewport
Block children always push their margin outside their parent, because `box-sizing` excludes child margins from the parent's area
The div's background only paints its content box, so any child margin is drawn outside it by the default rendering rules

rubric: Parent and first-child margins collapse when nothing (padding, border, BFC) separates them.
Distractors misstate background painting or box-sizing; backgrounds paint to the border box.

items.prompt: A header uses `position: sticky; top: 0` yet scrolls away with the page. Its ancestor `div.wrap` has `overflow: hidden` and the page itself scrolls. Which is the most likely cause?

options.label: Sticky only works when `z-index` is above 0, otherwise the browser treats the header as static and it scrolls away with the page
The `overflow: hidden` ancestor becomes the sticky element's scroll container and never scrolls, so sticking never triggers
The `top: 0` offset is measured from the start of the document, so the header sticks only after the whole page has scrolled past it
Sticky needs `position: relative` on its parent, so a tall parent without it is ignored when the browser works out the offset

rubric: Sticky positioning is relative to the nearest ancestor with overflow other than visible.
Distractors invent z-index or parent-position requirements.

items.prompt: A dropdown menu has `z-index: 9999` but renders beneath a positioned card with `z-index: 1` elsewhere in the page. The menu sits inside a `header` with `opacity: 0.95`. What best explains it?

options.label: `z-index` values above 999 overflow the browser's layer limit and are reset to 0, so the card's value of 1 outranks the menu
The menu needs `position: static` for its z-index to apply, so the card's positioned value beats the menu's higher number
Opacity below 1 takes the header out of normal flow, so its descendants are always painted below any element that has a z-index set
The header's `opacity` creates a stacking context, so the menu's z-index only competes inside it and the whole header ranks below the card

rubric: Opacity below 1 creates a stacking context that traps descendant z-index values.
Distractors invent layer limits or flow effects that do not exist.

items.prompt: A grid uses `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` in a 1000px container holding only 2 items. How does the result differ from using `auto-fill`?

options.label: Auto-fit collapses the empty tracks so the two items stretch across the row; auto-fill keeps the empty tracks and items stay near 200px
Both give identical layouts, since `1fr` always stretches items equally regardless of how many empty tracks remain in the row
Auto-fit wraps the two items onto separate rows at 1000px wide, while auto-fill keeps both on one row at 200px each
Auto-fit keeps five tracks and leaves three empty, while auto-fill collapses them so the two items stretch across the whole row

rubric: Auto-fit collapses empty repeated tracks to 0, letting `1fr` expand the occupied ones.
The strongest distractor swaps the two behaviours.

items.prompt: A child element has `height: 100%` but does not fill its parent. Which could explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The parent uses `box-sizing: border-box`, which disables percentage heights on all of its children
The parent's height is `auto`, so the percentage has no definite height to resolve against
Percentage heights only resolve when the parent's height is set in `px` rather than in `vh` or `%`
The child is absolutely positioned and a more distant ancestor is the nearest positioned one, so 100% refers to that box

rubric: Percentage heights need a definite containing-block height, and absolute children resolve against the positioned ancestor.
Distractors wrongly blame box-sizing or require px units.

items.prompt: On desktop, a long page shows a horizontal scrollbar though nothing looks wider than the window. On a phone with overlay scrollbars the problem does not appear. A full-bleed banner uses `width: 100vw`. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: `100vw` is measured from the parent's content box, so padding on `body` adds extra width beyond the viewport
Desktop browsers calculate `vw` from the monitor's screen width, so the banner exceeds any window that is not maximised
Overlay scrollbars on phones shrink the viewport, so the banner only overflows on desktops where scrollbars are hidden
`100vw` includes the width of the classic vertical scrollbar, so the banner is wider than the visible content area by that amount

rubric: `vw` includes the classic scrollbar's width, causing overflow only where scrollbars take space.
Distractors misdefine what `vw` is measured against.

items.prompt: Criteria: body text must scale with the user's browser default font-size setting, and nested components must not compound sizes. Which unit for `font-size` best meets both?

options.label: `rem`, since it scales from the root font size and never compounds through nested elements
`vw`, since it scales with the viewport and avoids inheriting anything from parent elements or user settings
`px`, since it gives the same predictable size in every component regardless of nesting depth or browser settings
`em`, since it scales from the parent font size and so respects the user's setting at every nesting level without surprises

rubric: `rem` honours the root setting and avoids compounding.
`em` compounds on nesting; `px` and `vw` ignore the user's default.

items.prompt: A product list has cards with unequal content. Criteria: titles, images and price rows must align across neighbouring cards in each row, with minimal extra markup and no fixed heights. Which approach is best?

options.label: Fixed `min-height` values on titles and images in each card, which keeps neighbouring rows aligned at every viewport width
Flexbox on each card with `flex: 1` on the title, which aligns every inner row across all of the neighbouring cards automatically
Grid on the list, each card spanning rows with `grid-template-rows: subgrid`, so inner rows align across cards without fixed heights
Floats with `clear: left` on every third card, so the rows of neighbouring cards share baselines across each row

rubric: Subgrid lets cards share the parent's row tracks, aligning inner parts across cards.
Flexbox inside each card cannot coordinate across sibling cards; fixed heights are brittle.

items.prompt: A stylesheet has `*:focus { outline: none; }` to remove the focus ring. Criteria: keyboard users must always see where focus is, and mouse users should not see rings after clicking. Which revision is best?

options.label: Keep the reset and use `:hover` to apply the same highlight, since hover and focus indicate the same interaction state
Replace it with `outline: 0 solid transparent` on `:focus`, so the ring is removed everywhere yet stays accessible to keyboards
Keep the reset and add `tabindex="0"` to all elements, so keyboard users can reach and see every control on the page
Remove the reset and style `:focus-visible` with a high-contrast outline, so keyboard focus shows but mouse clicks do not

rubric: `:focus-visible` shows indicators for keyboard modality while hiding them for most mouse clicks.
Other options keep focus invisible or confuse hover with focus.

items.prompt: The base layout is a single column; three columns are needed above 900px. Criteria: low-powered phones should parse the least override CSS, and adding further breakpoints should be easy. Which strategy is best?

options.label: Separate stylesheets for phone and desktop chosen by user-agent sniffing, so each device receives only the rules written for it
Desktop-first: base three-column rules, then `@media (max-width: 899px)` resets them, so small screens inherit the richest layout first
Only `max-width` queries stacked from widest to narrowest, since `min-width` queries cannot reliably override base declarations
Mobile-first: base single-column rules, then `@media (min-width: 900px)` adds columns, so small screens never undo wide-screen rules

rubric: Mobile-first keeps the base simple and layers enhancements, avoiding overrides on constrained devices.
Desktop-first forces small screens to undo rules; UA sniffing is brittle.

items.prompt: A 2400px-wide blog image displays at the full width of a 720px column on wide screens and full viewport width on phones. Criteria: no art direction needed, minimise bytes on small screens, let the browser choose the file. Which markup is best?

options.label: An `` with `srcset` using `x` descriptors, so the browser infers the displayed width from the screen's pixel density
A `<picture>` with one `<source media>` per breakpoint, so the browser picks a file size from the viewport width ranges
An `` of the 2400px file with `max-width: 100%`, so CSS scaling reduces the pixels the browser downloads
An `` with `srcset` listing several widths using `w` descriptors, plus `sizes` describing its layout width

rubric: `srcset` with `w` descriptors and `sizes` lets the browser pick the best file for layout width and density.
CSS scaling still downloads the full file; `x` descriptors ignore layout width.

items.prompt: Which are sound reasons to mark up a site's main menu with `<nav>` and its content with `<main>` rather than classed `div`s? Select all that apply.

options.label: Browsers apply built-in flex layouts to these elements, removing the need for layout CSS
Screen reader users can jump between landmark regions without tabbing through every link
The markup communicates structure to other developers, reducing reliance on class-name conventions
Reader modes and similar tools can identify primary content and skip repeated navigation
Search engines are guaranteed to rank pages higher whenever these elements are present

rubric: Semantic elements expose landmarks to assistive tech and tools, and document structure for maintainers.
Semantic elements add no default layout and give no guaranteed ranking boost.

items.prompt: A card component appears in a 300px sidebar and in a 900px main column on the same page at the same viewport width. Criteria: the card must switch from stacked to side-by-side based on the space it gets, with no per-page overrides. Which approach is best?

options.label: Add an `.in-sidebar` modifier class to the card and override the layout in sidebar contexts, so each placement is styled explicitly
Use `@media (min-width: 500px)` in the card's styles, so each instance reacts once the viewport is wide enough to fit it
Use `vw` units for the card's widths and padding, so the layout scales with the viewport and adapts equally in either column
Make the wrapper a size container and use `@container (min-width: 500px)` in the card's styles, so each instance adapts to its own space

rubric: Container queries respond to the component's container width, so identical viewports can yield different layouts.
Media queries and `vw` track the viewport, and modifier classes are per-context overrides.

items.prompt: A product grid must fill each row, keep cards at least 240px wide, and stretch the cards across the full row when only two exist. No media queries are allowed. Which `grid-template-columns` value best meets these criteria?

options.label: `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(240px, 1fr))`
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))`
`repeat(4, minmax(240px, 1fr))`
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 300px))`

rubric: `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks, so the `1fr` maximum lets the few cards stretch across the row.
`auto-fill` keeps empty tracks and leaves a gap. A 300px cap or a fixed count stops cards stretching or reflowing.

items.prompt: A disclosure toggle must work for keyboard and screen-reader users with the least custom code and the fewest ARIA workarounds. Which implementation is the best judgement?

options.label: A `<div>` with an `onclick` handler, a pointer cursor and an arrow icon, because clicking is the interaction users actually perform
An `<a href="#">` with a click handler calling `preventDefault`, because links are focusable and announced as controls
A `<button type="button">` toggling `aria-expanded` and the panel's `hidden`, because native buttons give focus and key handling
A `<span role="button">` with a click handler, because the ARIA role alone makes it focusable and operable by keyboard

rubric: A native button supplies focus, Enter/Space activation and role for free.
A role attribute adds semantics only, not behaviour. Links navigate and are the wrong semantics for a toggle.

items.prompt: A third-party widget stylesheet uses selectors like `#app .widget .btn.primary` and cannot be edited. Your overrides must stay maintainable, without `!important` escalation or specificity matching. Which approach is best?

options.label: Mark each override `!important`, since author `!important` declarations beat normal declarations from other stylesheets
Prefix each override with `#app` and repeat class selectors until it outranks the widget's rule, so specificity decides the winner
Place the widget CSS in an earlier `@layer` and your overrides in a later one, so layer order outranks its specificity
Load your stylesheet before the widget's, since the cascade favours the sheet that appears first in the document order

rubric: Cascade layers are compared before specificity, so later layers win without selector inflation.
Specificity races and `!important` escalate. Source order only matters at equal specificity, and the later rule wins, not the first.

items.prompt: Criteria: text must follow the user's browser default font-size setting, and sizes in nested components must not compound unexpectedly. Which unit strategy is the best judgement?

options.label: `em` for type and spacing, because each component then scales from its parent and keeps proportions consistent
`vw` for type, because it scales smoothly with the viewport width and removes the need for breakpoints
`px` for type with media queries, because fixed values give designers precise and predictable results
`rem` for type and spacing, because it follows the root font size without compounding in nested elements

rubric: `rem` is tied to the root size, which honours user settings and does not compound.
`px` ignores the user's setting, `em` compounds in nesting, and `vw` ignores the default font size.

items.prompt: A mobile landing hero must fill the visible screen so its call-to-action is not hidden behind collapsing browser toolbars, and it must still work in older browsers. Which declarations are best?

options.label: `height: 100%` on the hero alone, since percentages resolve against the visible screen without ancestor sizing
`min-height: 100vh; min-height: 100dvh;` so older browsers use the fallback and newer ones track toolbars
`height: 100vh` alone, since `vh` always equals the currently visible viewport height on mobile
`height: 100dvh` alone, since browsers that lack the unit simply substitute a sensible default height

rubric: The `vh` line is a fallback and `dvh` follows the dynamic viewport where supported.
`vh` can include hidden toolbar area. Percent heights need sized ancestors, and unsupported values are dropped, not replaced.

items.prompt: You are judging `:where()` for a design system's base styles that consumers must easily override. Which claims accurately support using it? Select all that apply.

options.label: It takes the specificity of its most specific argument, so it is a safe way to raise rule priority
An invalid selector in its list does not discard the whole rule, unlike a plain comma-separated list
It contributes zero specificity, so consumers can override base rules with any single class selector
It scopes the rule to a shadow tree so that outside stylesheets cannot override the declarations

rubric: `:where()` has zero specificity and uses a forgiving selector list.
Taking the most specific argument describes `:is()`. It has nothing to do with shadow scoping.

items.prompt: A vertical stack of cards in a flex column uses `margin-bottom: 1.5rem` on each card. Some cards are conditionally hidden, and the last visible card leaves extra space above the footer. Cards are reused elsewhere and must not need spacing overrides. Which change best meets these criteria?

options.label: Move the spacing to `padding-bottom` on each card, since padding never leaves trailing gaps
Set `gap: 1.5rem` on the flex container and remove the margins from the cards themselves
Add `.card:last-child { margin-bottom: 0 }`, which removes the trailing space whichever cards are hidden
Use `margin-top` on every card and trim the first one with `:first-child`, so hidden cards cannot matter

rubric: `gap` puts spacing in the parent and applies only between rendered items, so hidden cards cause no trailing space.
`:last-child` and `:first-child` still match elements hidden with `display:none`. Padding also leaves trailing space.

items.prompt: Markup order is header, main, aside, footer inside a wrapper. Constraints: the aside sits beside main and is at least 16rem wide, main takes all remaining width, and below 40rem of wrapper width the aside stacks full-width after main, with no media queries. Which wrapper rules meet all constraints?

options.label: `.wrap{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 16rem}`, which reflows by itself when space runs short
`.wrap{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(16rem,1fr))}`, which stacks columns when narrow
`.wrap{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap}` `main{flex:999 1 24rem}` `aside{flex:1 1 16rem}`
`.wrap{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap}` `main{flex:1 1 24rem}` `aside{width:16rem}`, which wraps the aside below main

rubric: A huge grow factor on main plus a 16rem basis on the aside gives a 40rem wrap point and a full-width stacked aside.
Fixed grid columns never wrap. A fixed-width aside stays 16rem when stacked. Auto-fit gives equal columns, not a dominant main.

items.prompt: Design a theme system: it must follow the OS preference by default, let users override it with a toggle that persists, and never flash the wrong theme on load. Which design meets all three constraints?

options.label: Two separate stylesheets, swapping the `<link>` href from a script on `DOMContentLoaded` once the saved choice has been read from `localStorage`
A `.dark` class toggled on `<body>` by a `defer` script that reads `localStorage` and falls back to `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')` when nothing is saved
A `prefers-color-scheme` media query only, since the OS setting already captures what each user wants at all times
Colour custom properties defaulting via `prefers-color-scheme`, overridden by `[data-theme]` set by an inline `<head>` script reading `localStorage` before paint

rubric: An inline head script sets the attribute before first paint, and CSS variables handle both the default and the override.
Scripts running after load cause a flash. A media query alone has no user override.

items.prompt: A responsive gallery shifts content as images load. Constraints: images scale to their container, each keeps its own aspect ratio without cropping, and space is reserved before the image loads. Which fix meets all of them?

options.label: Add `width` and `height` attributes with the intrinsic size and set `img{max-width:100%;height:auto}`
Set `img{height:300px;width:100%}` so every slot has the same fixed height before any image loads
Add a script that measures each image on `load` and then sets the height of its container to match
Set only `img{max-width:100%}`, since scaling to the container is enough to prevent any shift on load

rubric: The attributes let the browser compute an aspect ratio up front, and `height:auto` keeps scaling proportional.
A fixed height distorts or crops images. Without attributes or a ratio, no space is reserved. Script-on-load acts too late.

items.prompt: A `display:flex` row holds an icon and a long title. The title must stay on one line, end with an ellipsis, and never push the row wider than its container. Which rules on the title meet all three?

options.label: `min-width:0; overflow:hidden; text-overflow:ellipsis; white-space:nowrap;`
`overflow:hidden; text-overflow:ellipsis; white-space:nowrap;`, which truncate the text inside the flex item
`flex-shrink:0; overflow:hidden; text-overflow:ellipsis; white-space:nowrap;`, which fix the title width
`width:100%; text-overflow:ellipsis; white-space:nowrap;`, which let the title fill the row and clip itself

rubric: A flex item's automatic minimum width stops it shrinking below its content, so `min-width:0` is needed alongside the ellipsis trio.
Without `min-width:0` the item won't shrink, without `overflow` nothing is clipped, and `flex-shrink:0` forces overflow.

items.prompt: A proposal builds a modal as a `div` with `position:fixed`, a dimmed overlay, `z-index:9999`, a close button and an Escape-key listener. Which gap matters most for keyboard and screen-reader users?

options.label: It never moves focus into the modal or makes the page behind it inert, which `<dialog>` with `showModal()` provides
The `z-index` is too low, since modals need a value above every stacking context on the page
The Escape listener should be replaced by `tabindex="-1"` on the `body` to trap navigation inside the modal
The overlay should be `visibility:hidden` while open so assistive technology skips the dimmed backdrop

rubric: Without focus management and inert background content, keyboard users can tab behind the modal. A modal `<dialog>` handles both natively.
Stacking and the overlay's visibility don't address focus. `tabindex=-1` on body does not trap focus.

items.prompt: Assume a 16px root font size. Body text must be 1rem at viewports of 20rem (320px) or less, 1.5rem at 60rem (960px) or more, grow linearly between, and respect the user's root font-size setting. Which declarations meet every constraint? Select all that apply.

options.label: `clamp(16px, 12px + 1.25vw, 24px)`
`max(1rem, min(1.5rem, 0.75rem + 1.25vw))`
`clamp(1rem, 1.25vw, 1.5rem)`
`clamp(1rem, 0.75rem + 1.25vw, 1.5rem)`

rubric: The slope is 0.5rem over 40rem, which is 1.25vw, with a 0.75rem intercept. `max`/`min` is equivalent to `clamp`.
Without the intercept the growth does not start at 320px. The px version matches the numbers but ignores the user's root font size.

items.prompt: A team's article page must print without the navigation or its blank space, show each external link's address after its text, and never split a figure from its caption across pages. Which print stylesheet meets all three requirements?

options.label: `@media print{nav{visibility:hidden} a[href^="http"]::after{content:" (" attr(href) ")"} figure{break-inside:avoid}}`
`@media print{nav{display:none} a[href^="http"]::after{content:" (" attr(href) ")"} article{break-inside:avoid}}`
`@media print{nav{display:none} a[href^="http"]::after{content:" (" attr(href) ")"} figure{break-inside:avoid}}`
`@media print{nav{display:none} a::before{content:attr(href)} figure{break-after:avoid}}`

rubric: `display:none` removes the space, `::after` with `attr(href)` appends addresses, and `break-inside:avoid` on figure keeps it intact.
`visibility:hidden` leaves a blank gap, `break-after` does not keep a figure whole, and avoiding breaks inside the whole article is unworkable.
